question_en: Anand Rana, CFA, a portfolio manager for Amethyst Investment Group, expects that political conflict between two developed countries will create turmoil for emerging markets. He asks Rahul Kumar, CFA, a quantitative analyst at Amethyst, to develop a model to track various economic factors in each of the emerging markets. Kumar creates a model, tests it with available data from the last two years when emerging markets expanded rapidly, then delivers it to Rana. Unhappy with the finished product, Rana asks another quantitative analyst to create a model with different inputs. The new model, upon thorough testing by Rana, delivers more helpful results. Since this model delivers the results that Rana wants, he does not inquire how it uses the inputs or produces its results. Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis is most likely violated by:
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must deal fairly and objectively with all clients when providing investment analysis, making investment recommendations, taking investment action, or engaging in other professional activities." Standard III(B) Fair Dealing specifies that Members and Candidates must treat all clients fairly, specifically when disseminating investment recommendations or conducting an investment action on behalf of the client. When dealing with block trades involving multiple clients, all clients involved should receive the same execution price and be charged the same commission. This ensures that the potential for favoritism, or the perception of favoritism, is limited. Best practice suggests that managers and advisors inform clients of firm policies. However, even if clients agree to these policies, the Standard still requires that each client be treated fairly. Agreement to unfair policies does not permit the Member or Candidate to engage in practices considered unfair according to the Standards. In this scenario, Lindsay Grant violates the Standard by charging the endowment a lower commission than the foundations. The block order submitted by Grant included the orders for all her clients, so all should be treated equally. This includes being charged the same commission, despite the endowment being large enough to receive the lower commission on its own (Choice C). Grant should treat clients equally despite the Limestone Partners policy allowing for different commissions, since that policy is unfair under the Standard (Choice B).

question_en: Rul Investing is a full-service investment firm that has adopted the CFA Institute Code and Standards. As policy and practice, the firm prohibits communication between the research and investment banking departments. An exception occurs when the firm forms teams that include both research analysts and investment bankers to work on joint projects. For those projects, the entire team is eligible for a bonus based on the results of the project or transaction. The firm is careful to disclose to clients those cases in which research analysts and investment bankers work together. Does Rul's practice regarding these special project teams most likely comply with Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity?
option_b: No, since analysts can earn bonuses resulting from work on the special teams.
option_c: No, since the firm should not allow teams with both analysts and investment bankers.
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not knowingly make any misrepresentations relating to investment analysis, recommendations, actions, or other professional activities." Standard I(C) Misrepresentation prohibits Members and Candidates from knowingly using false or misleading statements in or omitting facts from any communication. Such misrepresentation can undermine investor trust. The Standard specifies that to violate it, a Member or Candidate must knowingly mislead, meaning that the Member or Candidate either has knowledge of or should have had knowledge of the misrepresentation or omission. In this scenario, Wei was not involved in the creation of her biography for the podcast. However, she promoted the podcast on social media and in marketing to prospective clients for months after recording it. In that time, she should have become aware of the error since it was about her work experience; therefore, by continuing to use the podcast without correction, she violated the Standard. Although Cheng included in the podcast's description a misrepresentation about Wei's role in creating exchange-traded funds, the error was unknown to her since the information came from a reliable source (ie, Cascade Partner's human resources manager). Therefore, Cheng had no reason to question the information's accuracy. As long as Cheng corrects the error if and when it becomes known to her, she will not have violated the Standard (Choices B and C).

question_en: One day after taking Level II of the CFA exam, Guyton Wyll visited a website used by several thousand CFA candidates and posted the following to a thread visible to candidates at all levels: "I can't believe that CFA Institute recommended that we study for more than 300 hours when they asked such easy questions on most topics. But the Ethics questions were so subjective, and I can't remember that any of them dealt with the Standards...really unfair!" Did Wyll's post most likely violate Standard VII(A)–Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs?
option_b: Yes, with his reference to the ethics questions
option_c: Yes, with his reference to CFA Institute's recommended study time
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must make reasonable efforts to ensure that anyone subject to their supervision or authority complies with applicable laws, rules, regulations, and the Code and Standards." Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors requires Members and Candidates who supervise employees to encourage behavior that complies with local laws, rules established by their firms, and the Code and Standards. They must also take reasonable steps to detect and prevent violations. Under the Standard, supervisors who supervise large numbers of employees are allowed to delegate supervision (Choice B). The employee to whom those supervisory responsibilities are delegated does not have to be a CFA charterholder (Choice C). However, the supervisor has the responsibility to instruct that employee on methods to promote compliance, including preventing and detecting violations. The supervisor still bears ultimate responsibility even though some day-to-day oversight has been delegated.

question_en: Trevor Halcott is a practicing lawyer and a CFA charterholder. He meets with the legal team of a potential client, Smith & Smith, Inc., to discuss a case that involves derivatives and portfolio management. At the beginning of the meeting, he hands out business cards that give his name as "Trevor Halcott, JD, CFA." Later, he tells the legal team, "completing the CFA Program greatly improved my knowledge of portfolio management and derivatives." Has Halcott violated most likely VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program?
option_b: Yes, by listing his JD before his CFA designation.
option_c: Yes, by stating that the CFA Program has increased his knowledge.
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in practices that distort prices or artificially inflate trading volume with the intent to mislead market participants." Standard II(B) Market Manipulation prohibits activities by Members or Candidates that distort securities prices. Manipulation can occur through Information-based activities, such as spreading false rumors, or Transaction-based activities, such as exaggerated trading between two accounts Manipulation can lead to a loss of trust in the fairness and integrity of the markets. The Member's or Candidate's intent determines whether he or she has violated the Standard. Actions that move security prices but were not intended to deceive market participants do not violate the Standard. In this scenario, Perrello Enterprises is reviewing acquisitions, so the statements made by Anabella Sanchez are not false or misleading. Sanchez did not intend to deceive or manipulate the market by issuing the press release. Her intention was to educate investors on the strategic direction of the company so they can make informed investment decisions, and therefore did not violate the Standard (Choices B and C). The fact that the press release caused an increase in the stock price does not mean the Standard is violated.

question_en: Bao Pham, CFA, is an investment adviser serving high–net worth retail clients. Several of Pham's younger clients prefer using instant messaging to communicate with him. Pham often receives requests and investment questions from clients via his personal phone and social media accounts. Pham does not forward any of these items to his firm since he considers them personal. The firm has no stated policy on data collection via personal devices or social media. Does Pham's conduct most likely comply with Standard V(C) Record Retention?
option_b: Yes, since the firm has no stated policy on the issue.
option_c: Yes, since these are private messages received through personal devices and accounts.
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in any conduct that compromises the reputation or integrity of CFA Institute or the CFA designation or the integrity, validity, or security of CFA Institute programs." Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs mandates that Members and Candidates act ethically when involved in any CFA Institute programs, including the CFA exams. The Standard prohibits behavior that compromises the public's confidence in the level of merit needed to achieve a CFA charter. It also encompasses CFA Institute's other credentialing programs. The Standard allows Members and Candidates to share opinions that disagree with CFA Institute policies (eg, allowing only two types of calculators) and stances on key issues (eg, advocacy articles). Members and Candidates are allowed to share opinions about the exams or CFA Institute as long as the opinions do not reveal specific information about the exams. In this scenario, since Jorge Martinez's post does not reveal confidential information about the exams, he does not violate the Standard, although he disagrees with CFA Institute (Choices B and C).

question_en: The endowment fund managers for Springvale University hire Omar Najjar, CFA, to provide investment advice. During their conversation, the managers mention that the endowment is funding a new academic building that the University has not yet announced to the public. Najjar tells the managers to call one of his clients, who just received an inheritance of $100,000 and disclosed that information to Najjar during a recent meeting. Later that night, Najjar has dinner with his friend, Farah Said, an alumna of Springvale University. Najjar tells Said that the University is planning a new academic building and needs donations. According to Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality, Najjar has most likely violated the Standard by disclosing:
option_a: his clients' inheritance to the endowment managers.
option_b: Springvale University's building plans and funding needs to Said.
option_c: both his client's inheritance and Springvale University's building plans and funding needs.
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must: Disclose to client and prospective clients the basic format and general principles of the investment processes they use to analyze investments, select securities, and construct portfolios and must promptly disclose any changes that might materially affect those processes." Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients requires members and candidates to disclose to current and prospective clients the basic format of investment processes and the limitations and risks associated with these processes. Members and candidates must use reasonable judgment when identifying important factors. To comply with the Standard, members and candidates should communicate to clients an understandable description of the investment process. It need not be a complete dissertation of the strategy. Here, Haughton must communicate, in understandable terms, the basic process and logic of the complex trading process. The communication should convey enough information that clients can recognize the risks and limitations of the investment process. (Choice A) Haughton is not required to communicate to current and prospective clients the entire complex trading strategy and its underpinnings. However, he must supply the basic premise of his strategy so that clients can gain an understanding of its limitations and risks. (Choice C) Describing significant trades is helpful information, but it is incomplete to meet this Standard. Current and prospective clients should be able to grasp the risks and drawbacks of the complex strategy.

question_en: The current market share information for the top 10 firms in an industry is shown in the image below: The industry's four-firm Herfindahl-Hirschman Index is closest to:
explanation_en: Oligopolistic markets are characterized by a small number of competitors selling nondifferentiated products. Kinked demand curves reflect the way competitors respond to any firm's attempts to increase market share or profitability. The dotted black demand curve shows the hypothetical quantities demanded for a single oligopolist's product assuming naïve responses by competitors to different pricing strategies. The adverse outcomes likely confronting oligopolists are reflected in the red and blue segments of the kinked demand curve (DED). Price cuts by one firm will likely be matched by competitors acting to defend their market shares. The result is less elastic demand (ie, red demand curve segment, D) at price levels below the initial equilibrium (E). Competitor reaction is quite different if oligopolists attempt to increase profitability by raising prices. The greater elasticity of demand (ie, the blue demand curve segment, D) at prices above the initial equilibrium results from competitors not matching a price increase. Some of the price- raising firm's customers switch suppliers to avoid the price hike. The unit sales decrease after a price hike will proportionally be greater compared with the unit sales increase if prices were cut. For example, whereas a 1% price cut might have resulted in a unit sales increase of 3%, a 1% price increase might cause a 5% decrease in unit sales. (Choice B) A monopolist is the only seller in their market segment. Monopolists are free to raise or lower price in search of profit maximization. (Choice C) Firms in purely competitive markets are price-takers. Each is so small relative to the total market that their actions cannot impact the equilibrium price; these firms therefore face flat (ie, infinitely elastic) demand curves.

question_en: Kinked demand curves are most likely associated with which type of market structure?
explanation_en: Oligopoly pricing theories Theory Description Compete on price Kinked demand curve Differentiate with advertising and branding Firms act independently and simultaneously Cournot assumption Equilibrium (ie, stable price and output quantity) No cooperation (ie, collusion) Nash equilibrium Firms act in their own best interest Firms act dependently and sequentially Stackelberg (ie, first mover) Leader (ie, top dog) sets quantity, others respond Firms cooperate to set quantity and price Collusion Firms act in the industry's best interest Oligopoly is a market structure in which a small number of firms sell similar products, with nonprice competition varying by market. For example, many consumer goods companies compete by differentiating products through advertising and branding. High barriers to entry typically protect existing firms from new entrants. Oligopolistic firms may adopt various pricing strategies. Since the Cournot assumption supposes a competitive market, demand and marginal revenue curves are downward sloping (ie, firms are not price takers). Supply and prices adjust naturally until, at long-run equilibrium, output quantity and price stabilize for each firm. (Choice A) The Stackelberg (ie, first-mover) pricing theory, not the Cournot assumption, supposes that firms act sequentially, with the market leader moving first. (Choice B) The Cournot assumption, applied to a duopoly (ie, two-firm market) in equilibrium, supposes that both firms act simultaneously and independently, without collusion (ie, cooperation), to determine production quantities to maximize profits.

question_en: Two firms, A and B, are the only manufacturers of Product X. Each firm can choose whether to charge a high or low price for X; currently both charge a low price. Each firm controls 50% of the market. The table shows the expected profit (in USD) for both companies at both prices: Based on this information, the Nash equilibrium for these firms:
option_b: exists when A charges a high price and B charges a low price.
option_c: exists when A charges a high price and B charges a high price.
explanation_en: A firm breaks even when total revenues are equal to total economic costs, and the firm earns an economic profit of zero. This condition holds for both perfect competition and imperfect competition (eg, monopolist competition, oligopoly, and monopoly). Economic profit is typically lower than accounting profit since economic costs include both accounting and opportunity costs (eg, owner's required return). Thus, a company may earn a positive accounting profit even if the economic profit is zero or negative. The breakeven point can also be expressed as when average revenue per unit equals average total costs per unit, which also results in an economic profit of zero: (Choices B and C) Firms incur both variable and fixed costs. Operating at a price equal to average fixed costs or average variable costs would mean that the firm was taking in revenue equal to its fixed costs or variable costs, thus not covering total costs. As noted, breakeven occurs when total revenue equals total costs.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.01 Firms and Market Structures - Answers.pdf
question_en: An analyst gathers current price and cost information about a firm operating in a perfectly competitive market: Based only on this information, which of the following is the firm's optimal course of action in the long run?
explanation_en: Collusion occurs when competing firms work together, either informally or by formal agreement (ie, a cartel), to maximize industry profits by reducing output and/or raising prices. For example, airlines may agree to charge the same price for specific routes, or oil producers may set output quotas. Collusion can be hard to maintain, however, as competitors have incentive to agree but then "cheat" and increase output and/or undercut the oligopoly price. Certain market characteristics tend to support successful collusion: A smaller number of firms means that coordination and monitoring are easier, and profits from any collusion will be divided among fewer firms. Where firms have similar cost structures, the firms face similar profitability hurdles, making it easier to agree on the oligopoly price. If products are homogeneous, the potential to compete through product differentiation is limited and collusion is more attractive. In this case, all four characteristics for Market A indicate a higher probability of successful collusion; only two characteristics of Market B and one of Market C suggest collusion would be successful (Choices B and C).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.01 Firms and Market Structures - Answers.pdf
question_en: For a duopoly (ie, two-firm market that is a special form of oligopoly) in equilibrium, which of the following choices best describes a characteristic of the Cournot assumption?
option_b: Firms cooperate to set output and price.
option_c: A firm's output is constant in the long run.
explanation_en: A firm operating under perfect competition maximizes economic profit by producing and selling at the quantity where marginal revenue (MR) equals marginal cost (MC). Cost in this context includes opportunity costs (eg, the owners' required return from the business). Perfectly competitive firms can earn economic profits in the short run, but even if economic profits are zero or negative, a firm may be earning an accounting profit. MR, the incremental revenue from selling one additional unit, depends on the firm's demand curve. In the case of perfect competition, the demand curve for any individual firm is a horizontal line at the market equilibrium price, since demand is perfectly elastic. Therefore, market price equals MR at all quantities (Choice C). MC, the incremental cost to produce one additional unit, depends on the firm's cost structure. Producing at a quantity greater than where MR = MC means that the incremental cost for each unit exceeds the incremental revenue generated by that unit and the firm generates a loss on each additional unit sold. Producing at a lower quantity means that the firm forgoes economic profit (in the short run) since the additional revenue from a unit sold would exceed the cost of the unit. (Choice A) Perfectly competitive firms can earn economic profits in the short run. However, in the long-run, the positive economic profits will attract new firms, which will increase supply/lower price until economic profit is zero. Note: Although this question specifically addresses perfect competition, the condition that firms optimally produce when MR = MC applies to all market structures. It is likely that the exam will have questions on this topic.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.01 Firms and Market Structures - Answers.pdf
question_en: If a firm is currently breaking even, it is most likely producing at the point where average revenue is equal to:
explanation_en: From an economic perspective, a firm breaks even when total revenues equal total economic costs and economic profit is zero, or (per unit) when average revenue equals average total cost (ATC). Total costs include both fixed and variable costs. Marginal revenue (MR) is the additional revenue generated from selling one additional unit, and marginal cost (MC) is the cost of producing one additional unit. With perfect competition, the firm has a horizontal demand curve, and therefore MR and average revenue are both equal to the market price. The breakeven point is when MR = ATC = MC; at this point, MR "covers" ATC, including fixed and variable costs. In the short term, fixed costs are sunk costs since fixed costs are independent of quantity produced. If the price falls so that MR < MC, the firm can continue to produce as long as MR is greater than or equal to average variable cost (AVC): since variable costs are still covered, there is still some profit from production (Choice A). However, if the price falls such that MR < MC < AVC, then the firm is not covering either its fixed or variable costs and should shut down. (Choice C) AVC is a component of ATC and therefore will never be equal, no matter how many units are produced.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.01 Firms and Market Structures - Answers.pdf
question_en: Characteristics for three oligopoly markets are as follows: Based only on this information, which of the markets has the highest probability of successful collusion?
explanation_en: A perfect competition market structure has many sellers, all of whom sell an identical product. Each seller's individual demand function (ie, demand curve) is perfectly elastic, meaning each can sell as many units of the product as it desires, but only at the market price. No seller in this market structure has the power to change the price. Although each seller's own demand function in a perfectly competitive industry is perfectly elastic, this is not the case for the industry's demand function. For nearly all products, as the price changes, the quantity demanded moves in the opposite direction, so the industry demand curve is negatively sloped. (Choice B) A perfectly price-elastic demand curve is horizontal. A perfectly elastic demand curve is the curve for each seller in a perfectly competitive industry. (Choice C) A perfectly price-inelastic demand curve is vertical. This means that there is a specific quantity demanded for the product that does not change, regardless of any change in price.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.01 Firms and Market Structures - Answers.pdf
question_en: A firm in a perfectly competitive industry increases production capacity, but then experiences an increase in its average total cost of production. To counteract the diseconomies of scale, the firm should most appropriately:
explanation_en: Perfectly competitive markets are characterized by numerous competitors selling an undifferentiated (homogenous) product. All firms are small relative to the total market for the product. Each can sell as much as they could produce at the market (ie, equilibrium) price. Additional output by one firm cannot impact the equilibrium price. Consequently, each faces an infinitely elastic or flat demand curve. Nothing prevents a firm from cutting the price of its output; however, doing so would not benefit the company. Unlike other industry structures, a firm operating in a perfectly competitive market could sell all it can produce at the market price. Selling at a below-market price implies forgoing profits. (Choice A) Unitary elastic refers to downward-sloping demand curves that reflect equal percentage changes in quantity and price (ie, a 1:1 ratio). Unitary elasticity means that the sensitivity of quantity demanded to changes in unit price varies across price levels. Trade-offs between price and quantity are typical for firms operating outside of purely competitive industries. Such firms can impact the demand for their product by raising or lowering price. (Choice C) Perfectly inelastic or vertical demand curves imply that the quantity demanded is unaffected by price. An example is demand for a drug that is currently the only effective treatment for a life-threatening disease. Perfectly inelastic demand is not a likely characteristic of any market in the long run.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.01 Firms and Market Structures - Answers.pdf
question_en: In the short run, a company maximizing profit in a market with perfect competition produces at a quantity that most likely results in:
option_b: marginal revenue equal to marginal cost.
option_c: market price greater than marginal revenue.
explanation_en: A firm's supply function reflects the quantities it will produce at various prices. All firms maximize profits at the level of output at which marginal cost (MC) = marginal revenue (MR); therefore, a firm's MC curve can be used to determine the optimal quantity of output. In a market with perfect competition, where a firm has perfectly elastic demand (ie, it is a price taker) and price (P) = MR, MC can also be used to determine the price that maximizes profit (ie, price at which MC = MR = P). Thus, the MC curve reflects the firm's willingness to supply and defines its supply curve. In other market structures, such as oligopoly, monopoly, and monopolistic competition, P ≠ MR due to inelasticity of demand. The optimal price is determined by the demand curve, which reflects the inelastic demand. Although MC can be used to determine the optimal quantity of output, the MC curve does not reflect the firm's willingness to supply at various prices and does not define the supply curve (Choices A and C). For a firm in perfect competition, long-run equilibrium means producing a quantity of output that minimizes the firm's average total cost, which equals the market price for its product. At this level of output economic profit is zero, so Total cost = Total revenue, or Price per unit × Quantity of units sold = Average total cost per unit × Units sold. Under the monopoly and monopolistic competition structures, firms have some pricing power, but any new price must be offered to all customers; therefore, MR ≠ Change in price multiplied × Change in quantity sold. Although the relationship between the average revenue and MR is similar under both structures, in general, the demand curve for monopolistic competitors is flatter (ie, more elastic).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.01 Firms and Market Structures - Answers.pdf
question_en: In the short term, for a firm operating under perfect competition, the most appropriate point for a shutdown is when:
option_a: marginal cost falls below average total cost.
option_b: market price falls below average variable cost.
option_c: average total cost equals average variable cost.
explanation_en: A firm's supply function reflects the quantities it will produce at various price (P) levels. Profit-maximizing firms produce output such that the incremental costs of the last unit produced (ie, marginal cost [MC]) equals the revenue received for that unit (ie, marginal revenue [MR]). Under perfect competition, individual firms cannot affect equilibrium (ie, market) price—they are "price takers"—so they face perfectly elastic demand curves. Therefore, the market equilibrium price is the firm's MR (ie, P = MR). All else equal, starting from equilibrium, if demand: increases and the equilibrium price rises, firms increase output, despite a rise in MCs, if the increase in cost does not exceed the additional revenue, or decreases and the equilibrium price falls, firms decrease output, thereby reducing MC to the point that the cost of the last item produced is no longer greater than the revenue from that unit. In the image, the quantities of output (Q and Q ) for two levels of demand (D and D ) also reflect the market equilibrium prices under perfect 1 2 1 2 competition, since P = MR. The bolded portion of the MC curve indicates how output varies between those price levels, or in other words, the quantities the firm is willing to produce (ie, its supply function) over that price range. (Choice A) Although the changes in variable cost are reflected in MC, it is the MC curve, not the variable cost curve, that is a firm's supply function. (Choice C) The average total cost (ATC) curve indicates average costs per unit as output varies but does not reflect how output changes as prices change.

question_en: In a perfect competition market structure, the industry demand curve is best described as:
explanation_en: Marginal cost (MC) is the increase in total expenditure for each additional unit produced. Marginal revenue (MR) is the increase in total revenue for each additional unit sold. Monopolists can offer products at a higher price, as demand allows, to increase total revenues, or at a lower price to expand unit sales. If there is no ability to engage in price discrimination, the lower price must be offered to all customers. MR accounts for the impact on total revenue of all units being sold at a new price. As shown in the image above, if monopolists produce and sell at quantities: between 0 and Q , MC is decreasing faster than MR, which increases profit margins and total profits. 1 between Q and Q , MC is increasing, which decreases profit margins; however, since MC is less than MR, total profits are still 1 pmax increasing. greater than Q , MC is greater than MR and total profits are reduced. pmax Therefore, total profit is maximized at the level of production at which MC equals MR. (Choices A and C) A marginal cost that equals either the average revenue or average total cost implies that production and sales levels are exceeding the profit-maximizing level of output (Q ). Cutting prices to expand sales beyond Q would increase revenue by less than the pmax pmax additional costs, thus reducing total profit.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.01 Firms and Market Structures - Answers.pdf
question_en: A firm operating in a perfectly competitive market has average variable costs of KRW 80,000 and average total costs of KRW 100,000. The market equilibrium price is KRW 75,000. Based only on this information, in the short run, the firm should most likely:
explanation_en: In the short run, firms in a monopolistic competition structure can earn an economic profit. Economic profit brings new entrants; the new entrants attract customers from existing firms. In the long run, this reduces demand for all firms that produce similar products, so the price falls until per- unit price equals per-unit cost. "Cost" in this context includes opportunity costs, and since the owners' return from the business is one type of opportunity cost, all firms' economic profit equals zero in the long run. In monopolistic competition, a firm maximizes profit when producing a quantity at which marginal revenue (MR) = marginal cost (MC). Producing a higher quantity means that the incremental cost for each unit exceeds the incremental revenue generated by that unit; the firm generates a loss on each additional unit sold. Producing a lower quantity (ie, minimizing marginal cost) means that the firm not only fails to maximize its economic profit in the short run, but actually incurs an economic loss (Choice C). Note: Although this question specifically addresses monopolistic competition, the condition that firms optimally produce when MR = MC applies to all market structures. It is likely that the exam will have questions on this topic. (Choice B) In monopolistic competition, profit maximization in the long run occurs when MR = MC, not when average cost is lowest.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.01 Firms and Market Structures - Answers.pdf
question_en: In perfectly competitive markets, each individual firm's demand curve is:
explanation_en: Oligopoly is a market structure characterized by a small number of firms (eg, airlines, beverage companies) selling similar products that are differentiated by advertising and branding. High barriers to entry (eg, initial capital investments, proprietary technology, patents, economies of scale) provide the firms with some or considerable pricing power. In an oligopoly, the small number of firms and their interdependence often results in economic profits, at least in the short term, which would typically attract other firms to enter the market. However, the existing firms are protected by the high barriers to entry. (Choice A) Structure A is a monopoly market, as indicated by high barriers to entry and a unique product. (Choice C) Structure C represents monopolistic competition, as indicated by many firms, low barriers to entry, and differentiated products.

question_en: If firms' supply curves can be used to determine the optimal, profit-maximizing price, those firms are most likely operating in:
explanation_en: Economic profit is the difference between a firm's total revenue, which is price (P) × quantity sold (Q ), and its total cost, which is cost (C) × E Q . Total cost consists of accounting expenses plus opportunity costs; opportunity costs include the owner's expected return from the E business. Any firm in a perfectly competitive industry should always produce the quantity of goods at which marginal revenue equals marginal cost. In the short run, a firm can earn an economic profit; this is reflected in the yellow rectangle shown above. However, since there are no barriers to entry in perfect competition, additional sellers are attracted by the potential economic profit and enter the industry. The increased supply from these new entrants causes the market price to fall to the point where marginal revenue, marginal cost, and average cost meet (Choice C). The new equilibrium quantity is at Q', which represents the point at which TR equals TC and economic profit equals zero. (Choice B) Economic profit equals accounting profit (ie, total revenue − accounting expenses) minus opportunity costs. Opportunity costs include a rate of return to the business owner. If economic profit equals zero, then the formula can be rearranged so that accounting profit = owner's return. This means that accounting profit is positive, not negative.
